lessons.title: Your first formula: operators and order
learn: Point and click instead of typing addresses
lessons.mac:
* = Shift + 8     ^ = Shift + 6     & = Shift + 7
Edit a formula in its cell: ⌃ + U
Fill down: ⌘ + D

steps.say: This is a furniture quote for Mehta Interiors. Every amount, the subtotal, the discount, GST and the grand total are formulas, so if a quantity changes, the whole quote updates. You'll build it with plus, minus, multiply, divide and brackets.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-01 Done

steps.say: You'll write formulas with the arithmetic operators, learn the order Excel calculates in, and point at cells with the arrow keys instead of typing addresses. The practice sheet is S03-01.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• + − * / ^ & and brackets
• The order Excel calculates in
• Point at cells instead of typing addresses

Practice sheet: S03-01

steps.say: Every formula starts with an equals sign. Excel uses a star for multiply and a slash for divide. It works out brackets first, then powers, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. It's the BODMAS you learnt in school.

acts.t:
Operators
+ add   − subtract   * multiply   / divide   ^ power   & join text   % percent

Order: ( brackets ) → ^ → * and / → + and − → &
Same as BODMAS, with powers before multiplying

steps.say: In D2, type equals. Now, instead of typing B2, press the left arrow twice. Excel points at B2 with a moving border and writes B2 into the formula for you.
Type a star for multiply, press the left arrow once to point at C2, and press Return. Twelve chairs at eight thousand five hundred rupees each is one lakh two thousand rupees.
Select D2 to D6 and press Command D to fill the formula down. Each row multiplies its own quantity by its own rate.

acts.h: Select D2:D6 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: In D8, add the five amounts: equals D2 plus D3 plus D4 plus D5 plus D6. The subtotal is two lakh eighty-one thousand two hundred rupees. In lesson three, SUM will do this faster.
The discount is five percent of the subtotal. In D9, type equals D8 star 5 percent. Excel understands the percent sign. Then in D10, subtract it: equals D8 minus D9.

GST is eighteen percent of the discounted amount, so in D11 type equals D10 star 18 percent. The grand total in D12 is equals D10 plus D11: three lakh fifteen thousand two hundred and twenty-five rupees.
Now try the grand total in one formula. In D13, type equals D8 minus D9 star 1.18, and press Return. Two lakh sixty-four thousand rupees. That's less than the discounted price, so something's wrong.
Excel multiplied before it subtracted, so it worked out D9 times 1.18 first. Put brackets round D8 minus D9: equals, open bracket, D8 minus D9, close bracket, star 1.18. Now the answer matches D12.

The ampersand joins text. In G2, type equals, then Quote for and a space inside double quotes, then an ampersand and G1. The cell reads Quote for Mehta Interiors, and it changes if the client's name does.

acts.h: Type ="Quote for "&G1 and press Return

steps.say: The caret raises to a power. If the chair rate grows six percent a year, the rate in three years is C2 times, open bracket, 1 plus 6 percent, close bracket, to the power 3. About ten thousand one hundred and twenty-four rupees.
Now prove it's live. Change the chair quantity in B2 to 15 and press Return. The amount, subtotal, discount, GST and grand total all update at once. Press Command Z to put it back.
On a Mac keyboard, the star is Shift 8, the caret is Shift 6, and the ampersand is Shift 7. To edit a formula you've already entered, press Control U.

acts.t:
Mac corner
* = Shift + 8     ^ = Shift + 6     & = Shift + 7
Edit a formula in its cell: ⌃ + U
Fill down: ⌘ + D

steps.say: To recap. Start with equals, and point with the arrow keys so you never mistype an address. Excel follows BODMAS, so use brackets whenever the order matters. And the ampersand joins text.

acts.t:
Recap
• = starts every formula; point with arrow keys
• Brackets → powers → × ÷ → + −  (BODMAS)
• & joins text, % works inside formulas

steps.say: Your challenge. In G6, work out the chair rate including 18 percent GST, with one formula that uses brackets. The answer is on S03-01 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
G6: the chair rate (C2) including 18% GST, in one formula with brackets.

Answer: sheet S03-01 Done

lessons.title: Relative, absolute and mixed references
learn: Why a formula breaks when copied
lessons.mac:
Toggle $ while editing: ⌘ + T  (or fn + F4)
Fill a selection: ⌘ + Return   •   Fill down: ⌘ + D   •   Fill right: ⌘ + R

steps.say: Here's GST worked out for six invoices from a single rate cell, and a discount price list where one formula fills the whole grid. Both depend on one idea: telling Excel which parts of a reference should move when you copy a formula, and which should stay put.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-02 Done

steps.say: You'll see why a formula breaks when you copy it, lock a cell with dollar signs using Command T, and use mixed references for a grid. The practice sheet is S03-02.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Why a formula breaks when copied
• $ signs with ⌘ + T
• Mixed references for a two-way grid

Practice sheet: S03-02

steps.say: A normal reference is relative: copy it down and the row changes, copy it right and the column changes. A dollar sign freezes the part that follows it. Command T cycles through the four versions.

acts.t:
References
A1     relative: column and row both move when copied
$A$1   absolute: nothing moves
$A1    column fixed, row moves
A$1    row fixed, column moves

⌘ + T while typing cycles: $A$1 → A$1 → $A1 → A1

steps.say: In C2, multiply the taxable value by the GST rate in F1: equals B2 star F1. Press Return. Twenty-two thousand five hundred rupees, correct.
Now fill it down to C7 with Command D. Every other row shows zero.

acts.h: Select C2:C7 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Select C3 and look at the formula bar: B3 times F2. Excel moved both references down a row. B3 is right, but F2 is empty, so the GST is zero.
Go back to C2 and type the formula again: equals B2 star F1. Before pressing Return, press Command T. Excel adds dollar signs, dollar F dollar 1, which lock the column and the row.
Fill down again. Every row now uses F1, and C3 shows fifteen thousand two hundred and twenty-eight rupees.

acts.h: Select C2:C7 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Change the rate in F1 to 12 percent, and all six rows update. Then press Command Z to go back to 18.
Now the price list. Each price is the list price in column B times 1 minus the discount in row 11. Select the whole grid, C12 to E16. We'll type one formula and send it to every cell.

Type equals B12, and press Command T three times. The first press locks both, the second only the row, the third only the column: dollar B 12. Column B must stay fixed whichever column the formula lands in.
Type star, open bracket, 1 minus C11, and press Command T twice to get C dollar 11, so row 11 stays fixed. Close the bracket, and press Command Return to fill all fifteen cells.

Check E16: dollar B 16 times 1 minus E dollar 11. Column B stayed, row 11 stayed, and everything else moved. The conference table at fifteen percent off is thirty-nine thousand five hundred and twenty-five rupees.
On a Mac, Command T toggles the dollar signs while you're typing a formula. F4 does the same, but most MacBooks need the Function key for it.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Toggle $ while editing: ⌘ + T  (or fn + F4)
Fill a selection: ⌘ + Return   •   Fill down: ⌘ + D   •   Fill right: ⌘ + R

steps.say: To recap. Relative references move when copied, which is usually what you want. Lock a single input cell with dollar signs. And for grids, lock just the column or just the row.

acts.t:
Recap
• Relative refs move when copied
• $F$1 locks an input cell (⌘ + T)
• $B12 and C$11: mixed refs fill a whole grid

steps.say: Your challenge. Add a 20 percent discount column: type 20 percent in F11, then fill F12 to F16 with the same mixed formula. The answer is on S03-02 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
F11: 20%
F12:F16: the same mixed-reference formula

Answer: sheet S03-02 Done

lessons.title: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and the COUNT family
lessons.mac:
AutoSum: ⌘ + ⇧ + T
Type =AV, then Tab: Excel completes =AVERAGE(

steps.say: This is a monthly sales summary for a twelve-person team: totals, the average, the lowest and highest sales, and four different counts. Six functions, and you'll see why three of them count different things.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-03 Done

steps.say: You'll total columns with AutoSum, use AVERAGE, MIN and MAX, and see how COUNT, COUNTA and COUNTBLANK differ. The practice sheet is S03-03.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• AutoSum with ⌘ + Shift + T
• AVERAGE, MIN, MAX
• COUNT vs COUNTA vs COUNTBLANK

Practice sheet: S03-03

steps.say: All of these take a range. SUM adds, AVERAGE finds the mean, and MIN and MAX find the smallest and largest. COUNT counts numbers only, COUNTA counts anything that isn't empty, and COUNTBLANK counts empty cells.

acts.t:
SUM(range)  total     AVERAGE(range)  mean of the numbers
MIN(range) / MAX(range)  smallest / largest
COUNT  numbers only
COUNTA  anything not empty (text too)
COUNTBLANK  empty cells
AutoSum: ⌘ + ⇧ + T

steps.say: Select C14, under the sales column, and press Command Shift T. That's AutoSum. Excel writes SUM and guesses the range above: C2 to C13.
Press Return. The team sold fifty-five lakh fifty-five thousand four hundred rupees this month.
Now D14, for customer visits. Press Command Shift T again and look at the range AutoSum guessed: only D11 to D13. It stopped at the blank cell in D10.
The range is still selected inside the formula, so just type D2 colon D13 and press Return. Always check what AutoSum picked before you press Return.
Now the summary. In G2, type equals AVERAGE, open bracket, C2 colon C13, close bracket. In G3, the same with MIN.
And in G4, MAX. The average sale is about four lakh sixty-three thousand rupees, the lowest is two lakh seventy-four thousand, and the highest is seven lakh two thousand.
Now counting. In G5, type equals COUNT of D2 to D13. The answer is 10. COUNT only counts numbers, so it skips On leave and the blank cell.
COUNTA counts anything that isn't empty, so G6 gives 11: ten numbers plus the words On leave. COUNTBLANK in G7 counts the empty cells: just 1.
For the team size, many people type COUNT of the names, A2 to A13. The answer is zero, because names are text and COUNT only counts numbers.
Use COUNTA for text. Type equals COUNTA of A2 to A13, and the team size is 12.
AutoSum's arrow on the Home tab also offers Average, Count Numbers, Max and Min. And if you select several columns plus the empty row below them, one AutoSum totals every column at once.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Home > AutoSum arrow: Sum • Average • Count Numbers • Max • Min
Select the numbers plus the empty row below, then ⌘ + ⇧ + T: every column gets a total

steps.say: On a Mac, AutoSum is Command Shift T. When you type a function name, Formula AutoComplete shows a list. Press Tab to accept the highlighted function and its open bracket.

acts.t:
Mac corner
AutoSum: ⌘ + ⇧ + T
Type =AV, then Tab: Excel completes =AVERAGE(

steps.say: To recap. AutoSum is quick, but check its range. AVERAGE, MIN and MAX ignore text and blanks. And use COUNT for numbers, COUNTA for anything, and COUNTBLANK for gaps.

acts.t:
Recap
• ⌘ + ⇧ + T, then check the guessed range
• AVERAGE, MIN, MAX skip text and blanks
• COUNT numbers • COUNTA anything • COUNTBLANK empty

steps.say: Your challenge. In G9, find the average number of customer visits. Think about which cells AVERAGE will include. The answer is on S03-03 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
G9: the average of the customer visits in D2:D13.
Which cells does AVERAGE skip?

Answer: sheet S03-03 Done

lessons.title: Rounding the right way
learn: ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, MROUND, CEILING, FLOOR, INT, TRUNC

steps.say: Rounding decides whether an invoice matches the books to the rupee. This sheet has eleven real situations, from GST to the nearest rupee to the number of cartons to order, each with the right function. On the right is a trap that catches a lot of people.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-04 Done

steps.say: You'll use ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, MROUND, CEILING, FLOOR, INT and TRUNC, and see why formatting a number is not the same as rounding it. The practice sheet is S03-04.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, MROUND, CEILING, FLOOR, INT, TRUNC
• Why formatting is not rounding

Practice sheet: S03-04

steps.say: ROUND takes a number and how many digits to keep. Zero means whole rupees, two means paise, and negative numbers round to the left of the decimal point. The others either force a direction or round to a multiple.

acts.t:
ROUND(number, digits)   0 = whole, 2 = paise, −3 = thousands, −5 = lakhs
ROUNDUP / ROUNDDOWN(number, digits)   always up / down
MROUND(number, multiple)   nearest multiple, e.g. ₹5
CEILING / FLOOR(number, multiple)   up / down to a multiple
INT(number)   down to the whole number below
TRUNC(number)   chops off the decimals

steps.say: In C2, GST on an invoice works out to 2,222 rupees and 46 paise. Type equals ROUND, open bracket, B2, comma, 0, close bracket. Zero digits means a whole rupee: 2,222.
In C3, round interest to the nearest paisa with two digits: equals ROUND of B3, comma 2. 456.789 becomes 456.79.

You need 250 units packed 24 to a carton, which is 10.4 cartons, and you can't order 0.4 of a carton. In C4, ROUNDUP of B4, comma 0, gives 11. In C5, ROUNDDOWN gives 10, the number of full cartons you can pack.
MROUND rounds to the nearest multiple. In C6, MROUND of B6, comma 5, turns 487 rupees into 485, the nearest five.
CEILING always goes up to a multiple, and FLOOR always goes down. CEILING of 487 to 10 is 490, and FLOOR is 480.
Digits can be negative. Minus 3 rounds to thousands, and minus 5 rounds to lakhs. In C9, ROUND of B9, comma minus 5, turns twelve lakh thirty-four thousand into twelve lakh.
INT drops the decimals of a positive number, so 7.83 years of service becomes 7 whole years.
But watch negatives. INT always goes down to the next whole number, so minus 7.83 becomes minus 8. TRUNC simply chops off the decimals, giving minus 7. For losses and refunds, choose on purpose.

Now the trap. E2 to E4 each hold 10.4, formatted to show no decimals, so they look like 10. Yet the total in E5 says 31. Ten plus ten plus ten looks like thirty, so on an invoice this looks like an error.

Formatting only hides decimals; the value is still 10.4. Select F2 to F4, type equals ROUND of E2, comma 0, and press Command Return. Then total them in F5. Now the total is 30, and it matches what you see.
Round where the business rounds. On an invoice, round GST on each line, then add the rounded lines, so the total on paper matches the total in Excel.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Round each line first, then total the rounded lines.
The printed invoice and the spreadsheet will then agree to the rupee.

steps.say: To recap. ROUND for normal rounding, ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN to force a direction, and MROUND, CEILING and FLOOR for multiples. INT and TRUNC differ on negatives. And formatting never changes the value.

acts.t:
Recap
• ROUND / ROUNDUP / ROUNDDOWN with digits (negative digits = thousands, lakhs)
• MROUND, CEILING, FLOOR round to multiples; INT vs TRUNC differ on negatives
• Formatting hides decimals; ROUND removes them

steps.say: Your challenge. In C13, round twelve lakh thirty-four thousand five hundred and sixty-seven rupees to the nearest thousand. The answer is on S03-04 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
C13: round B13 (₹12,34,567) to the nearest thousand.

Answer: sheet S03-04 Done

lessons.title: Formulas across sheets and files
learn: Link to another sheet and workbook

steps.say: This summary pulls April's sales from the April sheet, adds up the whole quarter across three monthly sheets with one formula, and brings in targets from another sheet. Change a number on any monthly sheet and the summary follows.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-05 Done

steps.say: You'll link to a cell on another sheet, handle sheet names with spaces, add up the same cell across sheets with a 3-D SUM, and see how links to another workbook look. The practice sheet is S03-05.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Link to another sheet
• Sheet names with spaces
• 3-D SUM across monthly sheets
• Links to another workbook

Practice sheet: S03-05

steps.say: A reference to another sheet is the sheet name, an exclamation mark and the cell. A 3-D reference names a first and last sheet, and covers every sheet in between.

acts.t:
Another sheet:        =Apr!B2
Name with spaces:   ='Targets FY27'!B2
3-D SUM:               =SUM(Apr:Jun!B2)
Another workbook:   ='[Targets FY27.xlsx]Targets'!B2

steps.say: The workbook has one sheet per month, Apr, May and Jun, all with the same layout. Pune's April sales are in B2 of the Apr sheet.

On the summary sheet, in B2, type equals, the sheet name Apr, an exclamation mark, and B2. The exclamation mark separates the sheet from the cell. Press Return: eighteen lakh forty-five thousand rupees.
Fill it down to B6 with Command D. Each branch picks up its own April figure.

acts.h: Select B2:B6 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: For the quarter, use a 3-D reference. In C2, type equals SUM, open bracket, Apr colon Jun, exclamation mark, B2, close bracket. It adds B2 on every sheet from Apr to Jun.
Fill it down. Pune's quarter is fifty-five lakh twenty-five thousand nine hundred rupees.

acts.h: Select C2:C6 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Targets are on a sheet called Targets FY27, with a space in the name, and names with spaces need single quotes. Leave out the closing quote and Excel refuses the formula with a message.

acts.h: Type ='Targets FY27!B2 and press Return

steps.say: Click OK, press Escape, and type it properly: equals, quote, Targets FY27, quote, exclamation mark, B2. Fill it down. If you build a link by clicking on the other sheet, Excel adds the quotes for you.

acts.h: Type ='Targets FY27'!B2 and press Return
Select D2:D6 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now a late invoice for Pune arrives in May. On the May sheet, change B2 to eighteen lakh twelve thousand five hundred. Back on the summary, Pune's quarter has gone up by fifty thousand.

A 3-D reference includes every sheet that sits between the first and the last. If someone drags a notes sheet between Apr and Jun, its B2 gets added too, so keep summary and notes sheets outside the range.

acts.t:
Watch out
=SUM(Apr:Jun!B2) adds every sheet positioned between Apr and Jun.
Keep summary and notes sheets outside that block.

steps.say: Links to another workbook add the file name in square brackets. In the Mac app, open both files, type equals, and click the cell in the other file. In Excel for the web, both files need to be in OneDrive or SharePoint.

acts.t:
Linking to another workbook
='[Targets FY27.xlsx]Targets'!B2
Mac app: open both files, type =, click the cell in the other file
Excel for the web: both files must be in OneDrive or SharePoint
Renamed or moved source? Data > Workbook Links to update it

steps.say: To recap. Sheet, exclamation mark, cell links to another sheet, with quotes when the name has spaces. SUM of first colon last sheet adds across sheets. And workbook links add the file name in square brackets.

acts.t:
Recap
• =Sheet!A1, and ='Sheet name'!A1 when there are spaces
• =SUM(First:Last!A1) adds across sheets
• [File.xlsx] in a link points to another workbook

steps.say: Your challenge. In E2 to E6, work out Achieved percent: the Q1 total divided by the Q1 target, as a percentage. The answer is on S03-05 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
E2:E6: Achieved % = Q1 Total ÷ Q1 Target

Answer: sheet S03-05 Done

lessons.title: Named ranges and the Name Manager
learn: Name a GST rate and use it everywhere
lessons.mac:
Formulas tab: Define Name • Create from Selection • Name Manager
Quick name: select the cell, type the name in the Name Box, press Return

steps.say: On this sheet, GST uses a cell named GST Rate instead of a cell address, and the zone totals read SUM of North, SUM of South. These are formulas you can read out loud, with one rate cell that drives the whole sheet.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-06 Done

steps.say: You'll name a single cell, use the name in formulas, create several names at once from headings, and manage them in the Name Manager. This lesson is recorded in the Excel desktop app, which has the same Formulas tab as Excel for Mac.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Name a GST rate and use it everywhere
• Create names from headings
• The Name Manager

Practice sheet: S03-06
Recorded in Excel desktop (same Formulas tab as Excel for Mac)

steps.say: A name is a label for a cell or range. Names start with a letter or an underscore, can't contain spaces, and can't look like a cell address. Names always point to the same place, so they never need dollar signs.

acts.t:
Named ranges
Rules: start with a letter or _, no spaces, not a cell address (GST18 is a cell!)
Formulas > Define Name • Create from Selection • Name Manager
Names are absolute: no $ needed

steps.say: Select G1, the GST rate. On the Formulas tab, click Define Name.
Type GST Rate, with a space, and click OK. Excel refuses, because the name isn't valid. Names can't contain spaces.
Click OK on the message, change the name to GST underscore Rate, and click OK. Refers to already points at G1 on this sheet.
In C2, type equals B2 star GST underscore Rate. As you type, the name appears in the AutoComplete list. Press Return.
Fill it down to C7. No dollar signs needed, because a name always points to the same cell. Then in D2, add B2 and C2, and fill that down too.

acts.h: Select C2:C7 and fill down with ⌘ + D
Select D2:D7 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Suppose the rate changes. Type 12 percent in G1, and every GST figure updates. Then put it back to 18 percent.
Now four names in one go. Select F3 to I9, the zone table with its headings. Click Create from Selection, tick Top row only, and click OK. Each column is now named after its heading.
In B11, type equals SUM of North. Then SUM of South, East and West in the cells below. Anyone reading these formulas knows exactly what they add.
Open Name Manager on the Formulas tab to see every name, what it refers to and its scope. You can edit or delete names here. Click Close.
On a Mac, the Formulas tab has Define Name, Create from Selection and Name Manager. The quickest way to name one cell is to select it, type the name in the Name Box, and press Return.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Formulas tab: Define Name • Create from Selection • Name Manager
Quick name: select the cell, type the name in the Name Box, press Return

steps.say: To recap. Name your inputs, like a GST rate, and formulas become readable. Create from Selection names whole columns from their headings. And Name Manager is where you check and tidy names.

acts.t:
Recap
• Name inputs: =B2*GST_Rate reads like a sentence
• Create from Selection: names from headings
• Name Manager: see, edit, delete names

steps.say: Your challenge. Name B2 to B7 Taxable, and in B8 total it with SUM of Taxable. The answer is on S03-06 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
Name B2:B7 'Taxable', then in B8: =SUM(Taxable)

Answer: sheet S03-06 Done

lessons.title: Every error value and how to fix it

steps.say: Every formula error in Excel starts with a hash sign, and each one tells you something different. On this sheet, eight broken formulas sit next to their fixes. Once you can read them, errors become clues instead of problems.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-07 Done

steps.say: You'll meet DIV zero, N A, NAME, REF, VALUE, NUM, CALC and SPILL, learn what causes each one, and fix them. The practice sheet is S03-07.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• #DIV/0!, #N/A, #NAME?, #REF!, #VALUE!, #NUM!, #CALC!, #SPILL!
• What each one means and how to fix it

Practice sheet: S03-07

steps.say: Here's the cheat sheet. Read the error, and it tells you where to look.

acts.t:
#DIV/0!   dividing by zero or a blank
#N/A        a lookup found no match
#NAME?     Excel doesn't recognise a word
#REF!       a reference that doesn't exist
#VALUE!    the wrong type of data, like text in maths
#NUM!       maths with no valid answer
#CALC!     a function had nothing to return
#SPILL!     a result has no room to spill

steps.say: Hash DIV zero means division by zero. B2 divides Shrikhand's revenue by its units, and none have sold yet. In C2, check first: equals IF, F2 equals 0, then 0, otherwise G2 divided by F2.
Hash N A means a lookup found nothing. Ghee isn't in our product list. XLOOKUP has a fourth argument for exactly this, so in C3 add Not listed, in quotes, as the if-not-found value.

acts.h: Type =XLOOKUP("Ghee 1 L",E2:E6,G2:G6,"Not listed") and press Return

steps.say: Hash NAME means Excel doesn't recognise a word in the formula. B4 says SUMM, with two M's. Fix the spelling in C4: equals SUM of G2 to G6.
Hash REF means a reference that doesn't exist. B5 asks INDEX for item 7 of a five-row list. You'll also see it after deleting a row or column that a formula used. In C5, ask for item 5.
Hash VALUE means the wrong type of data. B6 divides by F4, and F4 says 12 pcs, which is text. The fix is in the data, not in the formula.
Type just 12 in F4. B6 recovers on its own, and the same formula in C6 gives 120 rupees per unit.

Hash NUM means the maths has no valid answer, like the square root of a negative number in B7. In real sheets you'll see it from IRR or RATE when they can't find a solution. C7 takes the square root of 25 instead.
Hash CALC comes from the newer functions. In B8, type equals FILTER of the products where revenue is over one lakh. No product qualifies, so FILTER has nothing to return.
FILTER's third argument says what to show when nothing matches. In C8, type the same formula with None, in quotes, as the third argument.
Last, hash SPILL. In I2, type equals SORT of E2 to E6. The answer needs five cells going down, but I4 already has a note in it, so the result has no room.
Select I4 and press Delete. The sorted list spills into I2 to I6 straight away.
When you meet an error, select the cell and click the warning icon beside it. It names the problem and offers Show Calculation Steps, which walks through the formula one part at a time.

acts.t:
Reading the error
Select the error cell and click the warning icon next to it.
It names the problem and offers: Help on this Error • Show Calculation Steps • Ignore Error

steps.say: To recap. Each error names its cause, so read it before you change anything. Fix the data when the data is wrong. And use the built-in fallbacks, like XLOOKUP's if-not-found and FILTER's if-empty.

acts.t:
Recap
• Read the error: it tells you where to look
• Wrong data? Fix the data, not the formula
• Use fallbacks: XLOOKUP's 4th argument, FILTER's 3rd, IFERROR

steps.say: Your challenge. In C11, show Shrikhand's revenue per unit, G2 divided by F2, but show 0 instead of an error, using IFERROR. The answer is on S03-07 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
C11: =G2/F2 wrapped in IFERROR, showing 0 instead of #DIV/0!

Answer: sheet S03-07 Done

lessons.title: Auditing formulas
learn: Trace precedents and dependents, show formulas
Evaluate a formula step by step, Watch Window
lessons.mac:
Formulas tab: Trace Precedents • Trace Dependents • Remove Arrows • Show Formulas • Evaluate Formula • Watch Window
Show Formulas: ⌃ + `

steps.say: This is a one-page profit model. It looks fine, but the version you received had a hidden mistake that left out seventy-five thousand rupees of expenses. Excel's auditing tools found it in under a minute. Here's how.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-08 Done

steps.say: You'll show formulas, trace precedents and dependents, evaluate a formula step by step, and keep an eye on key cells with the Watch Window. This lesson is recorded in the Excel desktop app, which has the same Formulas tab as Excel for Mac.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Show Formulas, Trace Precedents and Dependents
• Evaluate Formula step by step
• The Watch Window

Practice sheet: S03-08
Recorded in Excel desktop (same Formulas tab as Excel for Mac)

steps.say: The tools sit together on the Formulas tab. Precedents are the cells a formula uses. Dependents are the formulas that use a cell.

acts.t:
Formulas tab > Formula Auditing
Trace Precedents: arrows from the cells this formula uses
Trace Dependents: arrows to the formulas that use this cell
Show Formulas (⌃ + `)  •  Evaluate Formula  •  Watch Window

steps.say: On the practice sheet, click Show Formulas on the Formulas tab. Every cell shows its formula instead of its result. Look at B11: B8 plus B9 plus 450000. A number typed inside a formula is a warning sign.
Click Show Formulas again to switch back to results.
Select B12, operating profit, and click Trace Precedents. Blue arrows point from the cells it uses: gross profit and total expenses.
Click it again to go one level further back. Now arrows run from salaries and rent into total expenses, but nothing comes from Other expenses in B10.
Click Remove Arrows. Then select B10 and click Trace Dependents. Excel says no formula refers to this cell. Other expenses of five lakh twenty-five thousand are missing from the total. Click OK.
Fix B11 with equals SUM of B8 to B10. Total expenses rise to forty-nine lakh sixty-five thousand rupees, and operating profit falls to fifty-two lakh twenty-eight thousand five hundred.
To see how a formula reaches its answer, select B13 and click Evaluate Formula. Each click on Evaluate replaces one part with its value: first B12, then B4.
One more click does the division: 19.5 percent operating margin. Click Close.
Now the Watch Window. Select B12 and click Watch Window, then Add Watch, and Add. The window floats over the sheet and shows B12's value wherever you are in the workbook.
Change the price in B3 to 1,500 rupees. The Watch Window shows operating profit jump at once. Then press Command Z to undo the change.
On a Mac, every one of these is on the Formulas tab. Show Formulas is Control and the backtick key, just left of the 1 on most keyboards.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Formulas tab: Trace Precedents • Trace Dependents • Remove Arrows • Show Formulas • Evaluate Formula • Watch Window
Show Formulas: ⌃ + `

steps.say: To recap. Show Formulas reveals numbers typed into formulas. Trace Precedents and Dependents show what feeds what, and a cell with no dependents can be a sign of a gap. Evaluate Formula and the Watch Window explain results.

acts.t:
Recap
• Show Formulas: spot typed-in numbers
• Trace arrows: an input with no dependents is a red flag
• Evaluate Formula steps through; Watch Window monitors key cells

lessons.title: Calculation settings and circular references
learn: Find and fix a circular reference
lessons.mac:
Formulas > Calculation Options: Automatic / Manual
Calculate now: ⌘ + =  or  fn + F9

steps.say: The company pays a ten percent bonus on profit after the bonus itself. That's circular, and Excel says so. This sheet solves it with a little algebra, and you'll also see how manual calculation can leave old numbers on screen.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-09 Done

steps.say: You'll compare automatic and manual calculation, then find and fix a circular reference. Error Checking and the calculation messages are shown in the Excel desktop app.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Automatic vs manual calculation
• Find and fix a circular reference

Practice sheet: S03-09
Recorded in Excel desktop (same Formulas tab as Excel for Mac)

steps.say: Normally Excel recalculates after every change. In Manual mode it waits until you ask. A circular reference is a formula that depends on its own result, directly or through other cells.

acts.t:
Automatic: recalculates after every change (default)
Manual: recalculates only when you press F9 (fn + F9, or ⌘ + =)
Circular reference: a formula that needs its own result
Fix: rewrite the maths. Use iterative calculation only on purpose

steps.say: Profit before bonus is twenty-five lakh rupees, in B1. The bonus is ten percent of profit after bonus, and B4 already subtracts the bonus in B3 from B1.
In B3, type the bonus the obvious way: equals B4 star B2. Press Return, and Excel warns about a circular reference. B3 needs B4, and B4 needs B3.
Click OK. B3 shows zero, and the status bar at the bottom names the circular cell. On a big sheet, Formulas, Error Checking, Circular References lists where they are.

Break the loop with algebra. If the bonus is ten percent of profit minus bonus, then the bonus is profit times ten percent, divided by 1.1. In B3, type equals B1 star B2, divided by, open bracket, 1 plus B2, close bracket.
The bonus is two lakh twenty-seven thousand two hundred and seventy-three rupees. D2 checks it: ten percent of profit after bonus gives the same figure.
Now the calculation setting. On the Formulas tab, open Calculation Options and choose Manual. People switch to Manual on very large, slow workbooks.
Profit is revised to thirty lakh. Type 3000000 in B1 and press Return. The bonus hasn't changed, and the status bar says Calculate. The numbers on screen are now out of date.
Press F9 to calculate now. On a MacBook that's Function F9, or Command equals. The bonus updates to two lakh seventy-two thousand seven hundred and twenty-seven rupees.
Switch back to Automatic straight away. A workbook saved in Manual mode can quietly show wrong numbers to the next person who opens it.

If a loop is truly intended, Excel can repeat the calculation until it settles. On Windows that's in File, Options, Formulas. On a Mac, it's Excel, Preferences, Calculation, Limit iteration. Use it rarely: a rewritten formula is clearer.

acts.t:
Iterative calculation (for intended loops)
Windows: File > Options > Formulas > Enable iterative calculation
Mac: Excel > Preferences > Calculation > Limit iteration
Prefer rewriting the formula: it's clearer and safer

steps.say: On a Mac, Calculation Options is on the Formulas tab too, and Calculate Now is Command equals, or Function F9.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Formulas > Calculation Options: Automatic / Manual
Calculate now: ⌘ + =  or  fn + F9

steps.say: To recap. Keep calculation on Automatic unless a workbook is too slow, and recalculate before you trust numbers in Manual. A circular reference means a formula needs its own result, and algebra usually breaks the loop.

acts.t:
Recap
• Automatic by default; in Manual, press ⌘ + = before reading numbers
• Circular reference = a formula needs its own result
• Break the loop with algebra; iterate only on purpose

lessons.title: Challenge 3: a sales commission sheet
learn: Totals, averages, rounding and an absolute rate cell

steps.say: Here's the commission sheet for a twelve-person sales team in Maharashtra and beyond. Sales are in, and the commission rate, two and a half percent, sits in H1. Your job is to finish the sheet.
The five tasks are on the right, from column J: commission with an absolute rate cell, rounding, totals, a summary, and a test of the rate.
Pause the video now and try all five tasks on sheet S03-10. When you're done, press play to watch the solution.

acts.t:
Your turn
Pause now and complete the five tasks on sheet S03-10.
Press play when you're done to see the solution.

Answers: sheet S03-10 Answers

steps.say: Here's the solution. Task one. In D2, type equals C2 star H1, press Command T to lock H1, and press Return. Then fill down to D13 with Command D.

acts.h: Select D2:D13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Task two. In E2, type equals MROUND of D2, comma 10, and fill down. Amit's commission of twelve thousand one hundred and eighty-three rupees seventy-five paise becomes twelve thousand one hundred and eighty.

acts.h: Select E2:E13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Notice D2 shows twelve thousand one hundred and eighty-four. That's only the format hiding the paise. E2 is the truly rounded figure.
Task three. Select C14 to E14 and press Command Shift T. AutoSum totals all three columns at once.
Task four. In H4 to H7, type AVERAGE, MAX and MIN of C2 to C13, and COUNTA of the names in A2 to A13.
Task five. Change H1 to 3 percent. Every commission, every rounded figure and every total updates, because they all point at H1.
Set it back to 2.5 percent.
Compare your sheet with S03-10 Answers. If the totals match, you've used every core formula skill from this section.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S03-10 Answers
